About: River-Boat Crossing

Source

Concept
Relative velocity in 2D — vector addition of independent components.
Serves
The one thing to notice: the current cannot change how long the crossing takes — only the across-stream component of the boat's velocity carries it over, so the current moves only WHERE it lands, never WHEN.
Inquiry
Which heading lands the boat exactly opposite its start? What does that heading cost in crossing time?
Misconception
"Rowing against the current gets you across faster." It does not — it only changes the landing point. Straight across is always the quickest crossing, and it is never the one that lands opposite.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Watch the crossing

The boat is aimed straight across the river (heading = 0°). Watch its ground trail (Pause / Play is in the top bar). Note the two readouts: crossing time (t) and drift (Δx).

The current is flowing left-to-right at 2 m/s. Where does the boat land, relative to its start?

2 · Predict — how to cancel the drift?

To land exactly opposite the starting point, what should the pilot do?

3 · Find the zero-drift heading

Now try it. Drag Heading — upstream from straight-across. Watch the drift readout — hunt for the heading where the drift flips sign, from downstream (+) to upstream (−). It crosses zero between 23.5° and 23.6°: the exact zero-drift heading is arcsin(vc/vbw) ≈ 23.58°, which sits between two slider steps.

Then look at the crossing time as you sweep the heading. Does it stay put, or does it change?

4 · Predict — does the current change the crossing time?

Hold the heading fixed at some angle. Now imagine you triple the current speed. What happens to how long the crossing takes?

5 · The one thing to notice

The current cannot change when you arrive — only where you land. The two components are independent:

• Across (y): only vbw·cos θ contributes → sets crossing time.
• Along (x): vc and vbw·sin θ contribute → set the drift.

So the fastest crossing (θ = 0) is never the one that lands opposite. You cannot have both.

01

At a glance

A boat sets out across a river that is also moving. The sim draws every velocity involved and the path the boat really follows, so you can see how the boat's own motion and the water's motion combine.

What you'll learn

  • How the boat's velocity relative to the water and the current's velocity combine into its velocity relative to the ground.
  • How the heading θ and the two speeds decide the crossing time t and the drift Δx.
  • How to choose a heading to land where you want.
The boat starts on the near bank and aims at an angle θ from straight across. The river is W wide and the current is vc.

What's on screen

  • River, top view: the near bank (start) at the bottom, the far bank at the top, and a current → arrow showing the flow. Its width is W = 200 m.
  • vbw: the blue arrow at the boat, its velocity through the water. The hull points along it.
  • vc: the amber arrow, the current, drawn from the tip of the blue arrow.
  • vbg: the green dashed arrow, the boat's velocity relative to the ground.
  • Trail: the path the boat has followed so far. A dashed start x line and a green ring marked opposite start sit directly across.
See itStart a crossing with the bow pointed straight across. Watch for: the boat leaving the near bank with three arrows at it, and a trail growing behind it.

03

The boat's ground velocity is a vector sum

The boat moves through the water with velocity v⃗bw, and the water moves past the banks with velocity v⃗c. Relative to the ground, the boat's velocity is the vector sum

v⃗bg = v⃗bw + v⃗c
The sim draws it tip to tail, with vbg closing the triangle.

Split each velocity along the two directions of the river. The heading θ is measured upstream from straight across.

  • Across the river: only the boat contributes, vbw cos θ. The current has no across part.
  • Along the river (downstream positive): vc − vbw sin θ, because the bow's upstream part subtracts from the current.
The across part of vbg is vbw cos θ. Its along part is vc − vbw sin θ.
See itStart a crossing with the bow turned 25° upstream and a fast current. Watch for: the hull pointing along the blue arrow while the trail follows the green dashed one.
04

Only the across part sets the crossing time

The boat reaches the far bank when it has covered the width W = 200 m in the across direction. Its across speed is vbw cos θ, so

t = W / (vbw cos θ)
vc does not appear.

The current flows along the banks, so it has no across part. It can carry the boat down the river but it cannot push the boat toward either bank, so it neither speeds up nor slows down the crossing.

  • Straight across (θ = 0) is the quickest crossing: t = W/vbw = 40 s for vbw = 5 m/s.
  • Turning the bow upstream shrinks cos θ, so t grows: 43.65 s at 23.6°, 80 s at 60°.
  • At θ = 20° the crossing takes 42.57 s whether vc is 0, 2 or 4 m/s.
See itCross at θ = 20° with vc = 4 m/s, then drag vc to 0 and to 2 m/s. Watch for: the crossing time t staying at 42.57 s while the drift changes.
05

The drift comes from the current and the bow together

The drift Δx is the along-the-river speed multiplied by the crossing time. The sim counts it positive downstream and negative upstream.

Δx = (vc − vbw sin θ) t
The current pushes downstream and the bow's upstream part pushes back.

With the bow straight across, nothing opposes the current, so Δx = vc t. For vc = 2 m/s and t = 40 s the boat lands 80 m downstream of the point opposite its start. At a fixed heading, a faster current gives a proportionally larger drift, because t stays the same. With vbw = 5 m/s and θ = 20°:

current vccrossing time tdrift Δx
0 m/s42.57 s−72.8 m
2 m/s42.57 s+12.3 m
4 m/s42.57 s+97.5 m

Even with no current the tilted bow carries the boat upstream of its start.

See itCross straight over with vc = 2 m/s. Watch for: the Drift readout at +80.0 m, and the trail bending to the right of the green ring.
06

Landing opposite needs a heading that cancels the current

Zero drift needs the bow's upstream speed to equal the current: vbw sin θ₀ = vc. That gives

θ₀ = arcsin(vc / vbw)
Possible only when vbw > vc.

For vbw = 5 m/s and vc = 2 m/s, θ₀ = arcsin 0.4 = 23.58°. The slider moves in 0.1° steps, so the drift reads +0.3 m at 23.5° and −0.1 m at 23.6°.

Landing opposite costs time. The across speed is now √(vbw² − vc²), so t = W/√(vbw² − vc²) = 43.64 s, against 40 s straight across. With any current (vc > 0), the quickest crossing is never the one that lands opposite.

If vc ≥ vbw, no heading cancels the current. The slider also stops at 80°, so θ₀ is reachable only while vc/vbw ≤ sin 80° ≈ 0.985.

vc θ

These sliders move the sim too.

See itCross with the bow at 23.6° upstream. Watch for: the trail running straight up the dashed start line to the green ring, and Drift near zero.
07

Where it matters

  • Rain and a walker. Rain falls straight down at 10 m/s. To a person walking at 5 m/s it arrives from ahead, tilted by arctan(5/10) = 26.6° from the vertical at 11.2 m/s, which is why an umbrella is tilted forward. It is the same triangle, with the walker's velocity in place of the current's.
  • Aircraft in a crosswind. A pilot flying at 200 km/h through air with a 50 km/h crosswind points the nose arcsin(50/200) = 14.5° into the wind to hold a straight track, and the ground speed is then √(200² − 50²) = 193.6 km/h.
  • Ferries and swimmers. For a given heading the crossing time ignores the flow, but the landing point does not. To land at a chosen spot the crew has to aim upstream, and that costs crossing time.
08

Summary

In one line. The boat's velocity relative to the ground is the vector sum of its velocity relative to the water and the velocity of the current.

Key points

  • Across the river the speed is vbw cos θ, so t = W/(vbw cos θ), and vc does not enter.
  • Along the river the speed is vc − vbw sin θ, so Δx = (vc − vbw sin θ) t.
  • Zero drift needs θ₀ = arcsin(vc/vbw), which exists only if vbw > vc.

Common mix-ups

  • "Aim upstream to cross faster." Turning upstream shrinks the across speed vbw cos θ. The crossing takes longer, and only the landing point moves.
  • "A stronger current delays the boat." The current has no across part. The crossing time is the same, and the boat just lands further along the bank.
  • "The boat travels the way its bow points." The bow points along vbw, but the path follows vbg. At θ₀ the path is straight across while the bow is tilted.

Things to try on your own

  • Keep vbw = 5 m/s and θ = 0, raise vc from 0 to 3 m/s in steps of 1, and divide each drift by vc.
  • Set vc = 3 m/s, work out θ₀ on paper, then set it and read the drift.
  • Set vc = 4 m/s and find the smallest vbw for which a heading up to 80° gives zero drift.
